title: Short-Run Costs
short: Fixed, variable and total cost, and the average and marginal costs computed from them.
trouble: Students compute marginal cost as total cost divided by quantity, or let fixed cost change with output.

blocks.html: Production (Short-Run Production) turns into costs once you pay for inputs. The costs a firm counts include implicit ones (Accounting and Economic Profit).

Fixed cost (FC) doesn't change with output in the short run; variable cost (VC) does; $TC = FC + VC$. Per unit: $AFC = FC/q$, $AVC = VC/q$, $ATC = TC/q = AFC + AVC$. Marginal cost is the extra cost of one more unit: $MC = \Delta TC / \Delta q$, which equals $\Delta VC / \Delta q$ because fixed cost doesn't change.

Marginal cost mirrors marginal product. If a worker costs \$20 an hour and the next worker adds 4 units an hour, those units cost \$5 each. When marginal product rises, marginal cost falls; once diminishing returns set in, marginal cost rises. That's why MC curves are U-shaped. Fixed cost has no "marginal" part: you pay it whether you make 0 units or 100.

blocks.title: From total cost to everything else
blocks.q: Using the table, find fixed cost, the variable cost of 4 units, the average total cost of 4 units and the marginal cost of the 5th unit.
steps: Fixed cost is total cost at $q = 0$: \$30.

blocks.title: Marginal cost from marginal product
blocks.q: A worker costs \$24 an hour. The next worker hired adds 8 units an hour. What is the marginal cost of those units?

blocks.html: Computing marginal cost as total cost divided by quantity (that's ATC), or letting fixed cost change with output. In the table, $TC(5)/5 = \$22$, but the 5th unit itself costs \$26. Check: MC is always a difference between two rows; averages are a division within one row.
